papers.title: Partitioned iterative FD-SPH for fluid-rigid-body interaction: Stability and validation for lightweight floating bodies
papers.abstract: This study assesses partitioned iterative fictitious-domain smoothed particle hydrodynamics (FD-SPH) for free-surface fluid-rigid-body interaction. Extending a strong-coupling framework for deformable structures, it combines volume-based hydrodynamic loads with Newton-Euler rigid-body updates. Within each time step, the mismatch between pressure-projected fictitious-fluid and rigid-body velocities is fed back iteratively. A fractional-step interpretation identifies conditions under which Passively Moving Solid (PMS) projection and Newton-Euler updates yield identical rigid-body velocities. Single-pass and iterative FD-SPH are compared under matched conditions. A two-dimensional settling-disk benchmark agrees with published results. In three-dimensional buoyancy-driven cube tests, single-pass coupling becomes unstable at specific gravities of 0.1 and 0.2. At 0.1, reducing the time-step size by a factor of 500 does not suppress the instability. Iterative strong coupling remains stable across the tested range of 0.1-1.0. Equilibrium heights and orientations agree with hydrostatic expectations and published stable configurations, respectively. Two- and three-dimensional wet-bed dam-break simulations reproduce experimental trends in wave elevation and floating-body heave and pitch. Two star-shaped rigid bodies demonstrate applicability to complex geometries without explicit interface reconstruction or surface-normal evaluation. All production strong-coupling simulations satisfy the prescribed relative-residual criterion at every time step before reaching the maximum coupling-iteration count. These results support iterative FD-SPH for lightweight and complex floating bodies in transient free-surface flows.

papers.title: A Volume of Fluid Immersed Boundary Method for Industrial Polymer Mixing
papers.abstract: Free-surface numerical simulation of polymer mixing processes requires handling rotating solid boundaries of complex shapes as well as kinematic viscosity ratios between polymer melt and air up to $10^8$. We present a finite volume method that couples a Volume of Fluid (VOF) interface-capturing scheme with a non-conforming immersed boundary (IB) method, so that moving screws are represented on a fixed mesh without remeshing. In standard segregated VOF solvers, part of the viscous stress is treated explicitly, which can lead to instabilities and severe time-step restrictions at such viscosity ratios. To address this limitation, we integrate into the VOF-IB framework a block-coupled (BC) scheme in which the full viscous stress, including its transposed-gradient part, is treated implicitly. The method is implemented in the finite volume library OpenFOAM. On a three-dimensional injection-molding test case with a generalized Newtonian melt, segregated solvers either diverge or produce spurious air-phase velocities at the time steps allowed by the block-coupled solver, which instead yields a physical solution and reduces the computing time by a factor of about 2.7 with respect to the fastest segregated run that remains physical. On the finer grid, the IB solution agrees with the conforming-mesh solution within 2% in velocity and 0.5% in pressure drop. The BC-VOF-IB solver is then applied to single- and twin-screw extruders under fully and partially filled conditions, capturing the filling dynamics and the resulting pressure build-up along the screw, demonstrating the applicability of the method to industrial geometries. The current formulation is isothermal; its extension to non-isothermal flows, required for quantitative prediction of melt temperature and viscous heating, is the subject of ongoing work.

papers.title: Flux-induced condensation in a radial geometry
papers.abstract: Stirring and shear usually suppress phase separation, but transport through a boundary can induce it. We study a binary mixture that is stable everywhere at rest and fills a two-dimensional annulus. The inner boundary is semipermeable and exchanges material with a permeate held at a fixed chemical potential, so that a steady flux of one component crosses the annulus. Although this driven system carries a steady current and produces entropy, within Model B dynamics its steady state is an equilibrium profile in an effective external field that is logarithmic in the distance from the center. Its strength is not imposed from outside but set by the permeate and the permeability of the boundary. Above a threshold driving flux, a condensed annulus forms around the inner boundary. It is bounded by a stationary front whose radius depends exponentially on the ratio of the bulk driving force to the flux. The front is pinned by the effective field and does not coarsen, and the threshold flux decreases only as the inverse logarithm of the system size. The driving flux shifts the phase lines but leaves the critical temperature unchanged. Interfacial tension gives rise to a critical nucleus and to a fold, at which the condensed state ceases to exist, with a threshold that we obtain in closed form. Numerical solutions confirm these predictions and reveal a hysteresis loop bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations. By symmetry, the theory also describes cavitation around a sink.

papers.title: Three-mode chimera-like states in a minimal network of active camphor ribbons
papers.abstract: Chimera states are a remarkable manifestation of symmetry breaking, wherein identical units spontaneously split into coherent and incoherent groups. The term "chimera" itself is inspired by the mythological creature having parts of different animals, reflecting the coexistence of distinct dynamical behaviors within a single system. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the existence of a three-mode chimera-like state in a system of four identical camphor-infused elliptical rotors, each pivoted at a corner of a square base. When placed on a water surface, the rotors self-propel and rotate due to Marangoni-driven flows. Chemical coupling mediated through the shared water interface gives rise to three distinct collective dynamical states, namely a synchronized one, an antisynchronized one and an incoherent one. Our results validate recent theoretical work about three-domain chimeras in reaction-diffusion models, providing new insights into nonlinear dynamics and suggesting that this new type of chimera may be observed in a broad class of physical systems.

papers.title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
papers.abstract: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability. Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests. Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

papers.title: Local velocimetry for atomic superfluids: from Riemann rarefaction waves to quantized vortices
papers.abstract: We demonstrate local velocimetry for atomic superfluids in two dimensions (2D). Using matter-wave interferometry based on Raman--Bragg beam splitters, we map the local gradient of the phase of the superfluid's wavefunction onto displacement of the interference fringes and reconstruct the 2D velocity field. We illustrate the capabilities of this technique by applying it to two canonical problems. First, we directly observe the self-similar evolution of the velocity field in 1D Riemann rarefaction flows. Second, we map out the full 2D velocity field around quantized vortices, explicitly demonstrating the quantization of velocity circulation.

papers.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
authors: Christopher L. Wirth (Case Western Reserve University)
papers.abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $\mu$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

papers.title: Activity-driven motion and deformation of a circular membrane domain
papers.abstract: Lipid bilayer membranes are nanometer-thin fluid interfaces characterized by both in-plane fluidity and lateral compositional heterogeneity. Cholesterol-rich liquid domains ("lipid rafts") are thought to regulate the spatial organization of membrane proteins and numerous cellular processes. While the passive diffusion and equilibrium shape fluctuations of membrane domains are well understood, much less is known about how the activity of molecular machines, such as protein pumps and enzymes, influences their mobility and deformation. Here, we analyze the dynamics of a membrane domain driven by an embedded molecular machine within the framework of two-dimensional Stokes flow. The molecular machine is modeled as a point singularity of the two-dimensional Stokes equations, including both rotational and irrotational singularities corresponding to force and source multipoles. We show that, despite being force-free, both force and source dipoles generate active flows that propel the membrane domain. For a force dipole undergoing rotational diffusion, the domain motion is diffusive at long times but exhibits a transient superdiffusive regime at intermediate times.

papers.title: Theory of magneto-electrokinetics in unidirectional electrolyte flow: Hydrodynamic potential and Hall effect
papers.abstract: We develop a theoretical framework for magneto-electrokinetic transport in dilute electrolytes under unidirectional flow and streaming current conditions. Unlike standard magnetohydrodynamics in liquid metals, where charge carriers are electrons and conductivity is typically uniform, electrolytes exhibit spatially varying ion densities and additional forces such as osmotic pressure. In steady state, the coupled Navier--Stokes, Nernst--Planck, and Poisson equations become analytically tractable. We derive a Boltzmann-like expression for ion distributions that incorporates both the electrostatic potential and a novel hydrodynamic potential arising from the magnetic field. This potential depends explicitly on the flow profile and is not screened close to the bounding walls. Applying the theory to Poiseuille flow, we derive expressions for the induced Hall potential and demonstrate its near-linear dependence on flow velocity and magnetic field strength, while remaining largely independent of salt concentration. To validate this one-dimensional framework, we analyze the two-dimensional spatial transients near the channel entrance. We demonstrate a separation of length scales: the Hall electric field and space charge adjust to the magnetic field almost instantaneously, whereas the macroscopic salt concentration wake develops over a much longer Graetz length dictated by the P\'eclet number. We also examine a similar flow with counterions only and no added salt, determining the resulting potential and ion distributions. This work offers new theoretical tools for understanding ion transport in microfluidic and electrochemical systems.

papers.title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part I: physical-space structures and energy variance budget
papers.abstract: Vertically resolved budget analyses of frozen moist static energy (FMSE) variance within a cloud-resolving model provide a rigorous perspective on the equilibrium state of deep convective self-aggregation. The analysis reveals that the variance budget is governed by a leading-order balance between vertical variance advection and the gradient term, which quantifies the coupling between vertical covariance FMSE fluxes and the mean vertical stratification. Because vertical FMSE covariance fluxes are strictly positive throughout the atmospheric column, the sign of the gradient term is entirely dictated by the vertical gradient of mean FMSE. The primary peak of variance production occurs at the boundary layer top, driven by the interplay between sharp FMSE gradients, intensified in dry regions where the moist boundary layer decouples from the dry free troposphere, and robust vertical covariance fluxes. The persistent positivity of these fluxes implies that moist (dry), high-energy (low-energy) anomalies are systematically tied to updrafts (downdrafts), regardless of the mean gradient sign. This breakdown of classical down-gradient mixing indicates that vertical transports are governed by non-local, long-distance interactions driven by large-scale overturning circulation. The large variance produced near the boundary layer top is subsequently transported upward and dissipated in the upper troposphere, where the gradient term turns into a sink. While radiation does not directly force local variance, it indirectly shapes the budget by establishing the mean stratification. Overall, local thermodynamic forcings are translated by the overturning circulation into the spatial redistribution of variance across multiple scales.

papers.title: Multi-scale dynamics of deep convective self-aggregation. Part II: scale-by-scale budget and mesoscale self-similarity
papers.abstract: This work investigates deep convective self-aggregation in the space of scales, extending the physical-space analysis of Part I. We introduce a novel theoretical framework by examining and deriving a generalized Yaglom equation for the second-order structure function $\langle \delta h_f^{\prime 2} \rangle$, the scale-dependent variance of Frozen Moist Static Energy (FMSE). Self-aggregation is found to be sustained by an inverse energy cascade driven by boundary-layer production and mediated by mesoscale circulations with horizontal scales $r \sim$(100-250 km). The inverse cascade of energy is found to be realized through a series of shallow and mid-level mesoscale circulations which behave in a self-similar way. Accordingly, the scale-energy variance exhibits an extraordinary collapse across all atmospheric layers onto a robust self-similar power law, $\langle \delta h_f^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{6/5}$. In contrast, horizontal velocity increments show a degree of self-similarity ($\langle \delta u_r^{\prime 2} \rangle \sim r^{2/5}$) that retains a residual height dependence. Interestingly, the FMSE scaling breaks down at elevations lower than 750 m and at small local scales below 100 km, allowing us to identify the boundary layer top as a scale-dependent dividing layer where the strong stratification filters the interactions between the surface and free-troposphere, so that small scale dynamics of the low and high atmospheric layers are decoupled while those at large mesoscale are coupled. The derived scaling laws are also used to quantify the moisture-convection feedback via scale-dependent correlation coefficients that show that vertical transport strengthens with scale ($\rho_{mc\perp} \sim r^{2/5}$), while horizontal convergence weakens at the exact inverse rate ($\rho_{mc\parallel} \sim r^{-2/5}$).

papers.title: Optothermal Actuation of Unidirectional Thermo-osmotic Flows
papers.abstract: In this paper, we experimentally demonstrate the microscale direction control of thermo-osmotic flows using a focused-laser heating. The key is the off-center laser irradiation on an immobilized light-absorbing microparticle, which generates a nonuniform, asymmetric heat source. The resulting thermo-osmotic flows are evaluated using the optically trapped particle tracking velocimetry (ot-PTV), presented in our preceding paper (T. Tsuji, et al., Physical Review Fluids 11, 034901 (2026)). It is shown that the flow characteristics can be modulated by the ionic strength of a sample solution and/or the surface molecular coating of the substrate. In particular, the significance of ionic strength on thermo-osmotic flows is discussed based on the surface potential of the substrate measured by frequency-modulated atomic force microscopy.

papers.title: Self-similar rupture of a thin viscous filament in a Hele-Shaw cell
papers.abstract: In this report, we shall revisit the rupture problem for thin filament in a Hele-Shaw cell. For a slightly perturbed interface with periodic boundary conditions, all modes of perturbation decay in such a way that the interface levels off and becomes flatter over time. On the other hand, if the two ends of the filament are pinned in place and fluid is withdrawn from each end with a sufficiently high outward flux, then the loss of fluid causes the filament to thin and ultimately to rupture at a finite time. This type of filament rupture has been studied at length, most notably in the 1990s. We illustrate typical solution behaviours, including infinite-time levelling and those that appear to approach symmetric and asymmetric rupture in finite time. For the symmetric case, we demonstrate how rupture is described by a similarity solution of the second kind. We briefly frame our results in a broader perspective by considering similarity solutions for the thin film equation with an exponent $m$, which reduces to the Hele-Shaw case for $m=1$, and comparing with recent results in the literature. This report presents the results of a project undertaken by the first author at the MATRIX Workshop \textit{Slow Viscous Flows with Interfaces}, 7--18 July 2025, under the supervision of the other authors.

papers.title: HAVAPlot: A Web-Based Scientific Visualization and Post-Processing Platform
papers.abstract: This paper presents HAVAPlot, a browser-based framework for scientific visualization and post-processing of numerical simulation data. Operating entirely within the user's browser, HAVAPlot requires no software installation or data uploads while supporting mesh-based and tabular datasets beyond computational fluid dynamics. The framework directly reads native OpenFOAM cases, including polyhedral meshes, ASCII and binary fields, boundary data, and Lagrangian particles, as well as legacy and XML VTK files and tabular datasets. It provides line, contour, and three-dimensional plots; exact polyhedral slicing; boundary extraction; variable calculations; customizable color scales; symmetry mirroring; zoomed insets; streamlines; isosurfaces; particle visualization; and vector PDF/EPS and data export. The underlying numerical algorithms are independently verified. Cell centers and volumes agree with an independent implementation of OpenFOAM's geometric algorithm, while 6.1 million field values across four two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional production cases are reproduced to machine precision. For analytical fields on distorted hexahedral meshes, cell-to-point interpolation exhibits second-order convergence in the interior and first-order convergence at boundaries. Meshes containing 250,000 cells load in at most 1.3 seconds. Applications to an impinging supersonic jet, hypersonic cylinder flow, a hybrid particle-continuum cold-spray nozzle, a three-dimensional gas-bearing film, and supersonic cone flow demonstrate the framework's capabilities.

papers.title: Onset of three dimensionality in transonic shock boundary layer interaction over a natural laminar flow airfoil
papers.abstract: The development of three-dimensionality in transonic shock--boundary-layer interactions (SBLI) can significantly influence the aerodynamic response of natural laminar flow (NLF) airfoils, yet the associated vorticity dynamics remain insufficiently understood. The present study investigates the short-time evolution of transonic SBLI over the SHM1 NLF airfoil using high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) simulations at three operating conditions reported by Fujino et al., Natural-laminar-flow airfoil development for a lightweight business jet, J. Aircraft 40, 609-615 (2003). The selected cases represent three distinct operating regimes: the initial development of a normal shock, drag divergence, and shock-induced separation. Comparisons with previously reported two-dimensional (2D) simulations establish the temporal interval over which the spanwise-averaged 3D flow remains close to the corresponding 2D evolution, while departures in surface pressure and skin-friction responses identify the subsequent development of 3D effects within the SBLI region. The temporal evolution of volume-integrated streamwise and wall-normal enstrophies further characterizes the development of the associated 3D vortical field. The compressible enstrophy transport equation (CETE) is subsequently employed to examine the mechanisms governing the evolution of the 3D vortical field. Viscous and compressibility-related terms dominate the normalized enstrophy budget during the early evolution, while vortex stretching remains a minor contribution in the normal-shock and drag-divergence regimes but becomes appreciable, albeit intermittently, with the development of shock-induced separation. Across the three operating regimes, the same principal enstrophy-transport mechanisms remain active, but their relative contributions to the normalized budget are redistributed with the SBLI topology.

papers.title: A branch-free three-dimensional ghost-cell immersed boundary method with direction-averaged extrapolation kernels
papers.abstract: Ghost-cell immersed boundary methods impose the wall boundary condition on a Cartesian grid by assigning values to the grid points just inside the body, the ghost points. A common approach reconstructs the ghost value from an image point, which requires a wall normal for every ghost point. Special treatments are also often required where the interpolation stencil leaves the fluid region, e.g., near thin, concave or highly curved parts of complex bodies. We present a ghost-cell method that needs neither wall normals nor image points. Instead of a single extrapolation direction, the method uses all fluid nodes within 2.5 grid spacings of a ghost point that satisfy a simple geometric condition. The ghost value is obtained as the average of one-dimensional linear extrapolations from these nodes through the wall crossings of the connecting segments. The weights depend only on the geometry and are computed offline as one kernel on a $5 \times 5 \times 5$ stencil per ghost point. The boundary treatment at run time is thus an explicit, branch-free weighted sum. For the flows around a sphere and the Stanford Bunny, a self-convergence study shows approximately second-order convergence of the velocity in the $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms. The maximum difference also decreases at second order for the sphere but more slowly for the Stanford Bunny, where it is observed at a few nodes next to the wall. The drag coefficient of the sphere at Reynolds numbers of 25--200 agrees with a previous study within 2.4% for 32 grid cells per diameter and 0.4% for 64. For the Stanford Bunny at a Reynolds number of 100, the force coefficients agree with a body-fitted solution within 1% for 64 grid cells per reference length, without any geometry-specific treatment. Although no pressure condition is imposed on the wall, the pressure field is smooth and consistent with the body-fitted solution.

papers.title: Effective-dimension estimation of a minimal turbulent channel flow via IRMAE-WD
papers.abstract: The implicit rank-minimizing autoencoder with weight decay (IRMAE-WD) (Zeng et al. 2024) aims to estimate the dimension of the low-dimensional manifold underlying high-dimensional data from a sharp drop in the latent singular values of a single trained model. We apply IRMAE-WD with a three-dimensional convolutional autoencoder to velocity fields of a minimal turbulent channel flow at ${\rm Re}_{\tau}=110$ and examine whether the drop represents the intrinsic degrees of freedom. We also compare the number of coordinates IRMAE-WD needs for a given reconstruction accuracy or smallest reproduced scale with that of proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). We find that a clear drop appears and that the reconstruction rate decreases by at most 0.01 percentage points with truncation at the drop. The drop thus marks the effective dimension of the trained representation. However, the drop position moves to the lower-dimension side as linear layers are added. In addition, the reconstruction error decreases only gradually with the number of coordinates in all but the smallest wavelength band. These results suggest that the drop position is set by the implicit regularization of the linear layers and cannot be regarded as the intrinsic degrees of freedom. In contrast, with transfer learning, the smallest number of coordinates needed for a given accuracy hardly depends on the number of linear layers and is smaller than that of POD up to a reconstruction rate of about 97%. IRMAE-WD also reproduces a given scale with fewer coordinates than POD. Above about 97%, however, POD requires fewer coordinates, mainly because IRMAE-WD reconstructs large-scale structures less precisely. Hence, when the error decreases continuously, as in the minimal channel flow, the number of coordinates needed to represent wall turbulence should be stated with the required accuracy or scale, not as a single number.

papers.title: Controlling the mixing efficiency in a rotating arc-wall mixer
papers.abstract: In the rotating arc-wall mixer, the flow through a plane channel is stirred by three segments of its walls, which rotate back and forth periodically, two in phase and the third in anti-phase. Using two-dimensional simulations of a Newtonian fluid, I study how the Strouhal number $St$ (0.25-8), the forcing ratio $\Lambda$ of the wall speed to the mean flow velocity (6.75-54), the Reynolds number $Re$ (0.1-20) and the Peclet number $Pe$ ($10^2$ up to the grid-limited regime) set the mixing efficiency and the chaotic transport that produces it. Throughout this range the fluid crosses a chaotic saddle without regular islands, so that mixing is limited not by a lack of chaos but by the fluid that crosses the mixer without being stretched much. The contrast of the stretching field, i.e., how unevenly the stretching is distributed, correlates with the efficiency better than the properties of the saddle ($r=-0.90$). The efficient periods lie in a window bounded by two kinematic conditions: every fluid parcel must see at least one reversal of the walls, and the fluid at mid-channel must be displaced by about one channel width per half period. Below the window, fluid escapes in pulses through the cells of an almost steady flow; above it, fluid is held near the arcs without being folded. The window closes below $\Lambda\approx7$ and moves to faster forcing as $\Lambda$ increases. Inertia strengthens the stretching but opens a weakly stirred wake, so that the efficiency is highest at moderate inertia ($Re\approx8$) and decreases beyond. The efficiency decreases only slowly with $Pe$, and a lamellar model based on the measured stretching extends the results to the Peclet numbers of applications. The energy cost grows as $\Lambda^2$ and does not depend on the period, which should therefore always be chosen inside the window.

papers.title: Scattering by Small Ice Crystals in Turbulence: From Orientation Statistics to Retrieval Biases
papers.abstract: Ice-cloud retrievals from polarimetric radar, lidar and submillimeter radiometry commonly assume random orientation, horizontal alignment or a prescribed flutter angle. We link the orientation dynamics of ice crystals to their scattering. Fluid-inertial torque turns small settling crystals broadside on, and turbulent velocity gradients turn them away, so their orientation depends on the dissipation rate. We combine a closed-form orientation distribution for overdamped spheroids, including rotational diffusion and turbulence intermittency, with orientation-averaged Rayleigh, Rayleigh--Gans, T-matrix and specular scattering. Turbulence enters the scattering only through the Legendre moments of the orientation distribution. In the Rayleigh regime the specific differential phase follows crystal alignment, so assuming perfectly horizontal crystals biases ice-water-content retrievals low. Combining the specific differential phase with differential reflectivity limits this bias to $25\%$ for a single size of the shapes studied. For size distributions that span the alignment transition the bound can fail, because the two observables weight sizes differently. Depolarization adds sensitivity to higher-order moments and to intermittency. At finite size the second orientation moment mainly controls the scattering cross sections and the asymmetry parameter, and for optically soft crystals its contribution vanishes $54.7^\circ$ from the vertical. Specular returns from partly aligned plates should persist for lidars pointed $3^\circ$ from nadir. An exploratory analysis of EarthCARE lidar data finds a weakly depolarizing, low-lidar-ratio signature most frequent near $-11^\circ$C, where plates grow. Degree-scale tilt widths inferred from glints and lidar require larger crystals, near or beyond the validity range of the model.

papers.title: The final stages of a Chapman-Jouguet detonation: support by its own products
papers.abstract: A planar Chapman-Jouguet detonation that runs out of fuel must become a shock. We show that, when the chemical energy decreases in the direction of propagation, the wave does not pass through the local Chapman-Jouguet states. The products of the richer mixture are at a higher pressure than the local Chapman-Jouguet state, so the wave is overdriven, it loses its sonic point, and forward characteristics carry the state of the rich products to the shock. The rarefaction behind the wave removes this support only if the distance travelled since initiation is small compared with the thickness of the fuel gradient, which is rarely the case. The wave speed instead approaches an envelope given by a Riemann problem between the rich products and the local mixture, ending at the Mach number of the shock transmitted into inert gas. For strong detonations this Mach number tends to a fraction $C$ of the Chapman-Jouguet value, with $0.621<C<0.625$ for every ratio of specific heats. The mechanism is purely gas-dynamic. Shock-fitted computations with a two-step chain-branching mechanism, for gradients 1 to 1000 induction lengths thick, confirm that no sonic point forms and that the induction zone never decouples.

papers.title: Bifurcation analysis of particulate Rayleigh-Benard convection
papers.abstract: Particles carried through a convecting fluid layer exchange momentum and heat with the fluid, and so change not only where convection starts but also how it saturates. We study this coupling in the particulate Rayleigh-Benard system, in which a dilute stream of thermally inertial particles is injected at one wall and removed at the other. An Eulerian two-fluid model retaining drag, pressure-gradient, added-mass, and buoyancy forces and interphase heat exchange describes heavy particles and bubbles through a single density parameter beta. After reproducing the linear stability results of Raza et al. (2025a), we use a multiple-scale expansion and a Fredholm solvability condition to compute the first Landau coefficient a1 near onset. At low and moderate particle loading, the bifurcation is supercritical for every density ratio considered, extending the conclusion of Srinivas and Tomar (2025) for very heavy particles. At higher flux, however, Re(a1) changes sign, and the onset becomes subcritical over a broad band of density ratios, from moderately heavy particles injected below their terminal speed to most light particles. In the plane of density ratio and injection velocity, this band is bounded by lines of tricritical points. Splitting a1 by the balance equation shows that its sign is set almost entirely by the fluid energy equation, while the direct nonlinear terms of the particle equations are five to six orders of magnitude smaller. The particles thus change the nature of the bifurcation indirectly, through the base state and the linear mode they help to shape, rather than through their own nonlinear dynamics.

papers.title: Swimming formula in a linearly viscous fluid with anisotropic and odd viscosity tensors at low Reynolds number
papers.abstract: We theoretically investigate the low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics of a microswimmer in a linearly viscous fluid. The fluid is characterized by a viscosity tensor containing both even and odd components, and can therefore exhibit anisotropic and chiral properties absent in an isotropic Newtonian fluid. By employing the generalized Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we establish the Onsager-Casimir reciprocity for the resistance tensors of an arbitrarily shaped rigid body. We then derive a swimming formula that linearly relates the swimming velocities to the prescribed surface velocity of a microswimmer and imposed background flows. As a showcase application of the derived swimming formula, we prove that the scallop theorem holds in this class of linearly viscous fluids. Furthermore, we investigate the equations of motion for a spherical swimmer in a fluid with odd viscosity, as a representative example of the generalized linear constitutive framework. In particular, we reveal that sufficiently strong shear flows destabilize the bimodal chirotactic alignment of a microswimmer. Our results highlight how intrinsic fluid chirality and anisotropy fundamentally alter the orientational dynamics and transport phenomena of microswimmers.

papers.title: Influence of an oxide cap on the combustion of aluminum particles using boundary-layer resolved simulations
papers.abstract: A distinctive feature of burning aluminum particles is the condensation of the primary combustion product, alumina, forming an oxide cap that covers part of the aluminum particle and alters the local combustion characteristics. This study systematically investigates the effects of an oxide cap on the combustion characteristics and interfacial processes of aluminum particles, using boundary-layer resolved simulations, considering variations in cap size, cap position relative to the flow direction, and the particle Reynolds number, $\mathrm{Re_p}$. The oxide cap modifies both the interfacial transfer and the surrounding combustion characteristics. Front caps enhance local evaporation near the junction between the cap and the aluminum body, whereas heat absorption by rear caps contributes to lower reaction temperatures. Variations in integrated heat release generally follow those in the evaporation rate. Based on the simulation results, the Lagrangian modeling framework was first revised for spherical particles. The film state is approximated using a 0.55-rule applied to temperature, species mass fractions, and pressure, from which the remaining thermophysical properties are derived. A simplified composition scheme enables film-state viscosity and fuel diffusivity to be pre-calculated as functions of temperature. Optimized Whitaker and Schiller-Naumann correlations were developed for the mass evaporation rate and drag force coefficient, respectively, showing good agreement with the simulation results. The framework was further extended to doublet particles with oxide caps. Accounting for the exposed aluminum area provides good evaporation predictions for rear caps, while front caps require a correction to the surface-averaged evaporation mass flux, particularly at high $\mathrm{Re_p}$.

papers.title: Lagrangian transport driven by travelling waves in a radially deforming circular cavity
papers.abstract: A travelling deformation of a circular cavity wall can carry particles with the wave or against it. For two counter-propagating waves of azimuthal order $m$ and amplitudes $a$ and $b$, the leading axisymmetric component of the total (Lagrangian) drift scales with the intensity difference $S_3=|a|^2-|b|^2$. We obtain the radial profile of the azimuthal drift in closed form in the viscous limit, where the Womersley number $\mathrm{Wo}$ tends to zero, and by quadrature for any finite $\mathrm{Wo}>0$. The total drift is the sum of the Eulerian mean velocity and the Stokes drift. For radial wall motion with $m\ge2$ and unequal wave intensities, the total drift follows the stronger of the two waves throughout the interior in the viscous limit, although the Stokes drift changes sign with radius for all $\mathrm{Wo}$. For $m=2$ and large $\mathrm{Wo}$, the predicted total drift just inside a radially moving wall opposes the wave to leading order in wall amplitude. For the same travelling shape, the total drift there follows the wave when the wall material also moves tangentially to preserve local arc length to first order. For the radial wall at large $\mathrm{Wo}$, the near-wall profile consists of the planar Longuet-Higgins result and a closed-form curvature correction. At large $m$ the core rotation approaches Tuck's finite-Reynolds-number waving-sheet result. At $m=2$ and $\mathrm{Wo}^2=10$, moving-domain simulations recover the leading-order drift coefficients for both wall motions.

papers.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FASTFarm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.

papers.title: Orientation dynamics of a settling spheroid in simple shear flow: bifurcations and stochastic alignment
papers.abstract: We investigate the orientation dynamics of a settling spheroid in simple shear flow, combining a deterministic dynamical-systems analysis with a stochastic Fokker-Planck treatment. The dynamics is governed by competition between the Jeffery torque from the shear and the inertial torque from settling. When gravity lies in the shear plane the equatorial great circle is invariant, and the azimuthal motion on it is overdamped motion in a tilted periodic potential controlled by a single parameter $\mathcal{R}$ combining shape anisotropy and settling strength. That reduced system undergoes a saddle-node bifurcation on an invariant circle at $\mathcal{R}=1$, with the period diverging as $(1-\mathcal{R})^{-1/2}$. For oblate spheroids the equator attracts and the bifurcation converts an attracting periodic orbit into an attracting in-plane equilibrium. For prolate spheroids the equatorial equilibria are transversely unstable and the vorticity-aligned director remains the attractor at every settling strength; rapid settling draws it onto an attracting broadside slow manifold. When gravity is parallel to the vorticity axis, a particle exhibits either log-rolling or tumbling motion, depending on its shape. Noise acts differently in the two cases. The oblate problem supports azimuthal winding, for which we obtain an exact reduced current and its Kramers limit, exponentially sensitive to the P\'{e}clet number; the prolate problem shows broadside excursions about a single nematic attractor, whose rate is set by a two-dimensional quasipotential not computed here. Asymptotics at small and large $\mathrm{Pe}$, with numerical Fokker-Planck solutions at arbitrary $\mathrm{Pe}$, quantify the orientation moments across all regimes.
